title: Making Business Sense of Quantum Hardware
gist: BCG finds enterprise quantum spending hit ~$550M in 2025, overtaking academia and government, and compares five hardware modalities (superconducting, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonics, spin qubits) on scaling, fidelity, coherence and clock speed. Fault tolerance via error correction remains the defining unsolved challenge, with timelines of 5-20 years, so firms should build a system-aware view and distrust raw qubit-count claims rather than bet on one modality now.

insights.claim: Enterprise spending on quantum computing reached about $550 million in 2025, surpassing total investment by academia and government for the first time, according to BCG research.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Signals demand shifting from public/academic to corporate budgets, supporting vendor revenue visibility.
insights.quote: enterprise spending reached new heights of about $550 million in 2025, surpassing total investment by academia and government for the first time
insights.locator: Despite the continuing uncertainties in technology

insights.claim: More than 90% of leading global finance and insurance firms, 56% of top health care and biopharma companies, and 52% of industrials companies are investing in quantum computing.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Financials are the most committed early adopters; sector penetration indicates where first commercial quantum demand will come from.
insights.quote: More than 90% of leading global finance and insurance firms, 56% of top global health care and biopharma companies, and 52% of industrials companies are investing in quantum computing
insights.locator: Despite the continuing uncertainties in technology

insights.claim: More than half of top companies across sectors, excluding consumer goods and real estate, have some form of quantum computing investment.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Quantum is becoming a mainstream corporate R&D line item outside consumer and real estate sectors.
insights.locator: Despite the continuing uncertainties in technology

insights.claim: The quantum industry's debate has shifted from whether the technology is feasible to which hardware architecture will be commercially viable and on what timeline.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Investor focus should move from 'if' to 'which modality wins', raising the stakes of platform selection among hardware vendors.
insights.quote: The debate has shifted from technology feasibility to hardware viability, specifically which architecture will define the commercial era and on what timeline.
insights.locator: The quantum industry’s center of gravity is shifting

insights.claim: There is no single quantum computer: five distinct hardware approaches (superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photon-based, and spin qubits) are advancing at different stages of maturity, each with different strengths and weaknesses.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Quantum exposure is not one bet; vendor-level outcomes depend heavily on which modality prevails.
insights.quote: there is no such thing as a single quantum computer
insights.locator: Despite the continuing uncertainties in technology

insights.claim: BCG evaluates quantum hardware on four factors: scaling (qubit count), addressability and noise (gate fidelity), coherence time, and clock speed, with every approach trading strength in one for weakness in another.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Provides a checklist for assessing quantum vendors beyond headline qubit counts.
insights.quote: Each approach trades strength in one area for weakness in another.
insights.locator: Four factors define how well a system

insights.claim: A two-qubit gate fidelity of 99.9% equates to one error per thousand operations, which is the key measure of how reliably the building blocks of quantum algorithms can be performed.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Fidelity thresholds are a concrete metric to benchmark vendor progress toward usable systems.
insights.quote: a two-qubit gate at 99.9% fidelity means one error per thousand operations
insights.locator: Addressability and Noise

insights.claim: A highly accurate but extremely slow quantum system may be impractical or no more useful than current supercomputers for computationally intensive tasks.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: High-fidelity but slow modalities face a real commercial ceiling against classical HPC.
insights.quote: A highly accurate but extremely slow system may be impractical, or no more useful than current supercomputers, for computationally intensive tasks.
insights.locator: Clock Speed

insights.claim: Since no hardware system leads on all four factors, matching tradeoffs to the intended use case is what separates a well-informed quantum strategy from a naive one.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Expect a multi-modality market segmented by application rather than a single winner in the near term.
insights.quote: This understanding separates a well-informed quantum strategy from a naive one.
insights.locator: Five Contenders

insights.claim: BCG groups the five systems into three maturity tiers: the proven leader (superconducting circuits), capable challengers (trapped ions and neutral atoms), and high-potential unknowns (photon-based and spin qubits); topological qubits are too early to compare.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Maps risk/maturity for quantum hardware vendor exposure by modality.
insights.quote: the proven leader (superconducting circuits), capable challengers (trapped ions and neutral atoms), and high-potential unknowns (photon-based and spin qubits)
insights.locator: In terms of maturity, the five systems

insights.claim: Superconducting quantum systems, backed by IBM and Google for more than a decade, are the dominant hardware today with the highest digital qubit counts, fast gate speeds, and a fabrication logic borrowed from semiconductor manufacturing.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Incumbents IBM and Google hold the most mature quantum platform position.
insights.quote: Backed by the likes of IBM and Google for more than a decade, it is in a maturity category of its own
insights.locator: Superconducting Circuits.

insights.claim: Superconducting qubits operate at about 15 millikelvin, requiring large dilution refrigerators and dense control wiring, and suffer from lagging fidelity, chip-geometry-limited connectivity, and hard wiring-density and thermal scaling problems.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Cryogenic and wiring supply chains are critical enablers and bottlenecks for the leading modality.
insights.locator: Qubits are fabricated on chips using loops

insights.claim: BCG argues that superconducting systems' scaling challenges are known challenges, and that this predictability is itself a competitive advantage.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Known engineering risk may deserve a lower risk premium than unknown-physics risk in rival modalities.
insights.quote: The engineering challenges at scale are real, but they are known challenges, which is itself a form of advantage.
insights.locator: The tradeoffs are well understood.

insights.claim: Trapped-ion systems achieve two-qubit gate fidelities at or above 99.9%, the highest of any system, with coherence times measured in minutes, but run four to five orders of magnitude slower than superconducting systems.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Trapped-ion vendors lead on quality but face a throughput handicap that may limit addressable workloads.
insights.quote: Trapped ions achieve two-qubit gate fidelities at or above 99.9%, the highest of any system, and coherence times measured in minutes rather than microseconds.
insights.locator: Trapped ions achieve two-qubit gate fidelities

insights.claim: Reaching the qubit counts needed for fault-tolerant computation remains a significant engineering challenge for trapped ions, partly because optical control systems add infrastructure complexity.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Scaling risk is the key diligence point for trapped-ion players.
insights.locator: Trapped ions achieve two-qubit gate fidelities

insights.claim: Neutral-atom systems offer long coherence and strong fidelity like trapped ions but, unlike trapped ions, have demonstrated a compelling path to scale.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Neutral atoms may be the challenger best positioned to combine quality with scale.
insights.quote: Unlike trapped ions, neutral atoms have demonstrated a compelling path to scale.
insights.locator: Neutral Atoms.

insights.claim: Neutral-atom systems enable quantum memory by moving atoms between computation and storage zones, which in current hardware makes error correction easier than on other platforms because idle qubits are shielded from ongoing computation.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: A structural error-correction advantage could accelerate neutral atoms' path to fault tolerance.
insights.locator: This system also enables a distinctive capability

insights.claim: Neutral atoms also support an analog computing mode that bypasses discrete logic gates, with researchers reporting real signs of quantum advantage in domains such as materials science, though precision is harder to control.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Analog quantum could yield earlier niche commercial wins in materials before digital fault tolerance.
insights.quote: researchers have reported real signs of quantum advantage in domains such as materials science
insights.locator: Neutral atoms also support an analog mode

insights.claim: Photon-based systems are natural carriers for quantum networking, but photon loss forces reliance on large qubit numbers with loss-tolerant error correction, and current systems are far from the million-qubit scale that may be achievable.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Photonics is a long-dated bet with a distinctive networking angle but significant scale and fidelity gaps.
insights.quote: million-qubit photonic systems may be achievable, but current systems are far from that scale
insights.locator: The scaling math for photonics differs

insights.claim: Spin qubits, built mostly in silicon, could eventually be manufactured on adapted existing semiconductor fabrication infrastructure, a high-volume production pathway that BCG says no other approach can credibly claim.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Spin qubits create optionality for semiconductor fabs and foundries to become quantum manufacturers.
insights.quote: a pathway to high-volume production that no other approach can credibly claim
insights.locator: The reason is that most spin qubits

insights.claim: Spin qubit systems currently have qubit counts only in the tens, but are compact enough to fit meaningful numbers on a fingernail-sized chip, giving them significant data center integration advantages over rack-sized optical setups or dilution refrigerators.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: If scaling is proven, spin qubits could be the most data-center-friendly modality.
insights.quote: Current qubit counts are in the tens for spin qubit systems.
insights.locator: Current qubit counts are in the tens

insights.claim: Despite being the newest entrant, spin qubits are in some respects the most strategically interesting hardware approach, with sound physics but an uncertain timeline.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: The least mature modality may carry the largest long-term upside.
insights.quote: In addition to being the newest entrant in the hardware race, they are in some respects the most strategically interesting.
insights.locator: Spin Qubits.

themes.theme: Fault tolerance and error correction race

insights.claim: Fault tolerance is the principal unsolved challenge for all quantum hardware: today's noisy systems can run some noise-tolerant specialized algorithms but error rates are too high for most commercially valuable algorithms.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Commercial value of quantum remains gated on fault tolerance; near-term revenue claims warrant skepticism.
insights.quote: The principal challenge facing all five hardware approaches—and quantum computing generally—is fault tolerance.
insights.locator: The Unsolved Challenge

insights.claim: Depending on the error correction code and error rate, a single logical qubit may require hundreds or even thousands of physical qubits for protection.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Headline physical qubit counts vastly overstate useful compute capacity.
insights.quote: a single logical qubit may require hundreds, or even thousands, of physical qubits for protection
insights.locator: The path to fault-tolerant computation

insights.claim: The quantum hardware race is not about who produces the most qubits but who produces qubits good enough and numerous enough to make error correction possible without an impractical number of physical qubits.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Evaluate vendors on qubit quality times quantity, not raw qubit roadmaps.
insights.quote: The race is not simply about which system can produce the most qubits
insights.locator: The developers of each hardware system

insights.claim: Trapped ions and neutral atoms need fewer physical qubits per logical qubit due to higher fidelity, superconducting systems compensate with speed and scale, and photonics builds error correction into its architecture from the start.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Different modalities reach fault tolerance via different levers, so progress metrics must be modality-specific.
insights.quote: Trapped ions and neutral atoms have fidelity levels that make error correction more efficient—they need fewer physical qubits per logical qubit.
insights.locator: On this dimension, the systems have

insights.claim: The milestone of a logical qubit outperforming its best constituent physical qubit has only recently been crossed and only in controlled conditions.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Fault-tolerant commercial scale remains distant despite headline breakthroughs.
insights.quote: has only recently been crossed and only in controlled conditions
insights.locator: An important error correction milestone

insights.claim: Forecasts for commercially useful fault-tolerant quantum computers range from five to 20 years depending on the hardware system tracked and engineering assumptions.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Long and wide timeline implies patient capital and high dispersion in quantum vendor outcomes.
insights.quote: Forecasts for commercially useful fault-tolerant quantum computers range from five to 20 years
insights.locator: The timeline depends on which system

insights.claim: Most quantum systems reach their qubit counts by linking modules, yet the vast majority of vendors report only module-level specifications, and BCG has observed module-to-module fidelities as low as 90% in some R&D systems.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Vendor specs may overstate whole-system performance; inter-module fidelity is a hidden diligence risk.
insights.quote: In some R&D systems, we have observed module-to-module fidelities as low as 90%.
insights.locator: Scaling—how many qubits a system

insights.claim: Every module boundary requires an electrical or photonic interconnect that can add latency, error, and control overhead, so the value of modular scaling depends on link quality and speed rather than the number of modules.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Quantum interconnect technology is a potential chokepoint and investable enabling layer.
insights.quote: The practical value of modularity will therefore depend on the quality and speed of these links, not simply the number of modules connected.
insights.locator: Scaling a quantum computer may ultimately

insights.claim: The quantum industry will need standardized metrics quantifying the performance impact of modularity, since cross-module effects on fidelity, connectivity, and error-correction efficiency are not captured in today's specifications.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Expect benchmarking/standards to emerge that could re-rate vendors whose modular performance disappoints.
insights.quote: The industry will need to develop standardized metrics that quantify the performance impact of modularity as systems scale.
insights.locator: Modularity adds another unresolved dimension

insights.claim: Most organizations do not need to bet on a specific quantum hardware system now, and doing so offers little advantage, but they should build a working system-aware view of the landscape.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Enterprise buyers likely favor cloud, multi-vendor access over hardware lock-in near term.
insights.quote: Most organizations do not need to place a bet on a specific hardware system now, and doing so offers little advantage.
insights.locator: The Implications for Companies Today

insights.claim: Quantum infrastructure decisions are not hardware-neutral: footprint, cooling, control complexity, and classical integration differ by system and drive capex/opex choices such as on-premise hosting versus cloud access.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Cloud-accessible quantum platforms benefit from enterprises avoiding modality-specific capex.
insights.quote: Infrastructure decisions are not hardware-neutral.
insights.locator: Infrastructure decisions are not hardware-neutral

insights.claim: Quantum vendor qubit-count comparisons are often misleading because they ignore fidelity, connectivity, and coherence; a 1,000-qubit superconducting system and an 80-qubit trapped-ion system cannot be compared directly.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/jean-francois-bobier
insights.so_what: Discount promotional qubit-count headlines when valuing quantum hardware companies.
insights.quote: A 1,000-qubit superconducting system and an 80-qubit trapped ion system cannot be compared apples-to-apples—and neither may be more capable for a given application.
insights.locator: Vendor claims require a hardware lens
